The California Association of Health Plans (CAHP), the Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies (ACLHIC), and America's Health Insurance Plans (AHIP), write that under the ACA, states are required to select an essential health benefit (EHB) plan that defines the health-related services and equipment that health plans and insurance policies must cover. The benchmark plan selected by the Legislature in California did not include hearing aids. CHBRP has confirmed that coverage for hearing aids and associated services mandated by this proposal would exceed EHBs, and therefore trigger the ACA requirement that the state defray the cost of additional benefit coverage for enrollees in QHPs in Covered California. CHBRP estimates that this bill could translate to a state-responsibility of $11,268,000 annually. It's also important to note that this would be the first time since the passage of the ACA that California could pass a coverage mandate that exceeds the EHBs. The opposition is concerned about the precedent that this action may set, which could trigger a slew of new mandates to be introduced that exceed the EHBs, requiring more state funding to defray these costs. While these reforms have provided both large and small investors increased flexibility and cost savings, it is also true that the improved market access can be "gamed" in a manipulative manner. A copyright story published on August 23, 2001, in the Seattle Times noted described a form of spoofing in the stock markets: The National Association of Securities Dealers (NASD) PageM is investigating 11 cases of possible "spoofing" by brokers who try to manipulate stock prices by entering false quotes and then canceling them. Traders' use of these so-called "phantom quotes" has persisted even as regulators have tightened surveillance of the Nasdaq Stock Market and filed charges against seven brokers and investors since 1998, NASD Executive Vice President Stephen Luparello said in an interview. The NASD, a self-policing brokers' group, also has referred 21 other possible spoofing cases for Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) inquiry in the last 2-1/2 years, including two this past May, he said. "The integrity of the market suffers from this practice because the quotes indicate that something might be happening with a stock when it's really just manipulation," Luparello said. Spoofing, which can be considered fraud, typically occurs on thinly traded Nasdaq stocks with wide spreads, Luparello said. 6. However, the Attorney General is still concerned about the potential harmful effect of allowing disclosure of what would otherwise be privileged information between attorney and client under the aegis of "improper governmental activity." The definition of the phrase (which earlier included phrases drawn from Rule 3-600, such as "a violation of law reasonably imputable to the organization"), the Attorney General argues, leaves the interpretation of what is improper governmental activity to the individual attorney and his or her personal and political views. "While we may all agree that certain conduct, such as the Quackenbush mis-administration (sic) of the Department of Insurance, should see the light of day, we may have legitimate differences of opinion about whether a governmental activity is "likely to result in substantial injury to the organization," involves "willful misuse of public funds" or "breach of fiduciary duty," or involves the "willful omission to perform" an official duty. The proposed exceptions?will unwisely empower attorneys representing public agencies to act as free agents subject to their personal viewpoint, and place them in a state of perpetual conflict with their clients, chilling the trust and open access to information essential to their profession and compromising their effectiveness." [Letter from the Attorney General's Office, dated June 27, 2002.] The Attorney General suggests limiting the definition of "improper governmental activity" to "conduct that constitutes or would constitute a felony." With this definition, the AG states, there would be little difference between attorneys in interpretation of conduct that should clearly be reported. The Attorney General makes a good point. A broad definition might embolden publicity-seeking disclosures by loose cannons, to the detriment of the government agency. However, their suggested amendment may narrow the bill too much. For example, it is not clear if an agency official who used a government charge card to purchase a personal item during official travel is guilty of a felony. A possible consequence of that narrow amendment is a spate of future legislative measures to upgrade current misdemeanors to felonies, just to protect the government attorney whistleblower. There are other phrases used in the Government Code that also may be used to limit these exceptions to the attorney-client confidentiality rule, such as conduct that is "willful or corrupt misconduct in office" that would be grounds for removal of a public official from office. [Government Code Section 3060 et seq.] This phrase has been extensively interpreted in case law to apply to situations that would appear to be "improper governmental activity" as defined by , although the situations are limited to local agency officials, including school district officials. has been amended to remove from the definition of "improper governmental activity" undefined violations of law "reasonably imputable to the organization" or "likely to cause substantial injury to the organization," which, under Rule 3-600, could trigger an attorney representing an organization to take actions consistent with Section 6068(e) or, if necessary, resign. Thus "improper government activity" includes conduct that is less definitive than a felony, as the Attorney General would prefer, but would fall under "willful or corrupt misconduct in office," "willful or breach of fiduciary duty," "willful misuse of public funds," and conduct constituting "crime, fraud, or serious and willful violations of law." In all of the above cases, the improper governmental activity should probably be tied to substantial harm to the public interest, so that the attorney would be compelled to take the protected actions in order to prevent or rectify the improper governmental activity. Anthem Blue Cross (Anthem) states that this bill sets up an Exchange framework that is inconsistent with the concept of consumer choice by requiring the exchange to "determine health benefits." Furthermore, Anthem states that the PPACA already establishes benefit tiers and "essential health benefits" for the individual and small employer markets, whether coverage is purchased inside or outside the Exchange, and that having the Exchange "determine and approve benefit designs" is duplicative of federal requirements and will only serve to further limit consumer choice. Anthem writes that this bill makes the Exchange an "active purchaser," thus allowing it to set prices. Anthem states that the PPACA already establishes a rate review process for premiums charged in the individual and small group markets, which will be executed by the CDI and DMHC. Anthem states that if both the regulators and the Exchange are responsible for approving rates without a consistent process, the rates for the same product could be different inside and outside of the Exchange, violating the federal requirement that the entire market be treated as a single risk pool. Finally, Anthem asserts that setting rates in the Exchange would likely politicize the rate- setting process, which has proven to lead to insurer insolvency and insurers withdrawing from the market, reducing choices for consumers. Anthem suggests amending this bill to remove these provisions and instead clarifying that regulation of health plan and insurance products sold through the exchange are the sole purview of the CDI and DMHC. The Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies (ACLHIC) writes that the Exchange appears to have the power to negotiate rates for the products sold within the Exchange, and at the same time, requires participating carriers to offer the same products outside the Exchange. ACLHIC is concerned that these negotiated rates may not be actuarially sound and place participating carriers at a market disadvantage with nonparticipating carriers. ACLHIC states that participating carriers should compete on quality and price. ACLHIC also writes that there is already extensive criteria for carrier certification to participate in an Exchange included in PPACA, and will be further expanded when federal rules come forward, and that additional and potentially conflicting state standards may serve to limit the choice of plan in the Exchange. ACLHIC argues that, given the robust certification criteria that will already apply, any carrier that can meet those criteria should be eligible to participate in the Exchange. The California Hospital Association (CHA) is concerned over the provision in this bill that specifically expand the role of County Organized Health Systems beyond the original scope and purpose. CHA states that without a compelling reason to do so, it could be premature to provide for government-operated health plans to offer commercial coverage in the private health insurance market

Compline provides this information in a user-friendly, electronic format on a subscription basis to hundreds of insurance agents and brokers in California. As existing law does not provide for information service companies to have direct access to ex-mod information gathered by the WCIRB, Compline's current source of ex-mod information is through admitted workers' compensation insurers. These insurers are statutorily required to share information on their policyholders with the WCIRB, and, in turn, they can access, in hard copy, WCIRB's consolidated statewide data concerning employer ex-mods and related information. The sponsors state that this bill is necessary in light of plans by the WCIRB to institute a new, on-line system that will allow the WCIRB to provide information, including ex-mod information, electronically to member insurers and agents and brokers who subscribe to the system. This new system is very similar to the system that information service companies currently have in place. The sponsors argue that unless information service companies, such as Compline, can obtain the same information, in the same format and at the same time as the WCIRB intends to release it, information service companies will be unable to compete. The result, sponsors contend, will be that the WCIRB, a quasi-public entity created to collect, compile and analyze data required to be submitted to it from every admitted workers' compensation insurer, will be the exclusive provider of ex-mod information and other related information. The sponsors assert that establishing the WCIRB as the sole provider of this information was not the Legislature's intent, nor was it their intent to allow the WCIRB to develop an exclusive for-profit franchise to sell information to workers' compensation insurance agents and brokers. The sponsors argue that this bill will maintain a competitive market in the business of providing access to workers' compensation ex-mod and other related information, which is used by insurance agents and brokers to facilitate the placement of workers' compensation insurance on behalf of their clients. Without this legislation, the sponsors assert that competition in providing access to this information will be drastically reduced or eliminated

The author further amended the bill to permit the grand jury, through a joint request with the attorney general or the district attorney, to close the grand jury proceedings to the public when necessary, subject to the approval by the presiding judge of the superior court. The author of the bill states that this measure will "[promote] accuracy and thoroughness in grand jury proceedings." Witness' Proposed Right to Counsel: As noted above, this bill would also allow a witness before a civil grand jury proceeding who is or becomes the subject of a grand jury investigation to have an attorney present under specified conditions during his or her testimony. This section of the bill is identical to an earlier measure, AB 527 (Baugh), which was passed by the Legislature in 1999, but then vetoed by the governor. Proponents of the measure contend that in the absence of having counsel present an uninformed witness may inadvertently waive his or her essential rights, or may hesitate to testify entirely because of fear of being without guidance. Existing law prohibits the attorney for a witness to be present during his or her testimony before the grand jury. The only persons who are allowed to be present during grand jury proceedings are members of the grand jury, prosecutors, and necessary personnel such as a court reporter and an interpreter. (Section 939.) While the attorney for a witness is prohibited from being present during a client's testimony, witnesses before the grand jury do have a right to confer with counsel during the proceedings. The counsel waits outside the hearing room and any time the witness wants to confer with counsel he or she is permitted to do so. Commenting on the impracticality of this practice, the author of the bill highlights: Often the witness will have retained counsel, but counsel must remain outside the room resulting in an almost comedic routine of the jurors asking a question, the witness leaving the room to consult with counsel, and then returning to answer the question. The United States Supreme Court has stated that the constitutional right to counsel attaches at the initiation of adversary proceedings. (Kirby v. Illinois, 406 U.S. 682, 688 (U.S. 1972).) The Court noted that, "the right to counsel exists to protect the accused during trial-type confrontations with the prosecutor." (United States v. Gouveia, 467 U.S. 180, 190 (U.S. 1984).) The California Supreme Court addressed concern over the potential for abuse of the grand jury process, noting: "The prosecuting attorney is typically in complete control of the total process in the grand jury room: he calls the witnesses, interprets the evidence, states and applies the law, and advises the grand jury on whether a crime has been committed. The grand jury is independent only in the sense that it is not formally attached to the prosecutor's office

When Governor Davis vetoed this proposal contained in AB 527 in 1999, he stated: The current operation of the grand jury, which follows English common law practice, has remained essentially unchanged since California was admitted to the Union in 1850 and has served us well for 150 years... Thus, any major departures from existing practice warrants thorough and thoughtful consideration and debate within the legal community and among legal scholars. In response to the governor's veto, legal scholars at the "Capital Center" noted above conducted a study on the potential reform of California's grand jury system. (Vitiello & Kelso, Reform of California's Grand Jury System, supra at 515.) At the conclusion of its study the Capital Center observed (supportive of the merits of this provision in the measure): Counsel has a role in assuring that a target makes proper invocation of such [constitutional] rights and privileges. Counsel may also encourage some targets to testify. This offers the grand jury a fuller understanding of the facts than might otherwise have been available. The end result increases the grand jury's ability to exercise independent judgment on whether to indict. . . . [T]he creation of the right to counsel furthers independence of the grand jury and . . . serves the public's interest, and not merely the interest of the target. Additionally, twenty years prior to Governor Davis' veto of AB 527 the American Bar Association (ABA) conducted an investigation of the grand jury system, concluding after several years of study that "a witness before the grand jury shall have the right to be accompanied by counsel in his or her appearance before the grand jury." (American Bar Association, Grand Jury Policy and Model Act (1977-1982) (Marcia Christensen ed., 2d ed. 1982) [hereinafter ABA Report].) The ABA commented that limiting the role of counsel would prevent the grand jury from becoming a "mini-trial," but would address concerns about the unfairness of disallowing a witness from being accompanied by counsel. The ABA study went on to observe: Requiring a witness who needs advice of counsel to consult his attorney outside the grand jury room door is awkward and prejudicial. It unnecessarily prolongs the grand jury proceedings and places the witness in an unfavorable light before the grand jurors. The American Law Institute has called it a "degrading and irrational" procedure. It is extremely damaging to the witness continually to get up, go outside, and consult with counsel. This sentiment was reflected in the testimony of former Watergate Special Prosecutor Charles Ruff when he testified before the House Judiciary Subcommittee in 1977, declaring: The mere possibility of occasional disruption simply cannot overcome the right of the individual witness to consult his attorney without going through the mildly absurd process of leaving the grand jury room every time. Indeed, most prosecutors would admit, I think, that they count on the burden of leaving the room to dissuade the witness from asserting his right to counsel." (Testimony before House Judiciary Subcommittee, April 27, 1977, at 3.) Allowing Witnesses to Have an Attorney Present During Grand Jury Testimony Would Put California In Line with the Practices of Other States: A state- by-state study conducted by the United States Department of Justice, and later updated by the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers (NACDL) reveals that twenty-one states, including Arkansas, Colorado, Utah, Nevada, Florida, New York, and Kansas allow some witnesses to have counsel present during grand jury proceedings. (NACDL, State by State Information Sheet¸ available at http://www.nacdl.org/grandjury. Furthermore, this proposed section of the measure appears to conform to the recommendations of the American Bar Association, put forth in a comment to a Judicial Advisory Committee of the Administrative Office of the United States Courts. Kansas additionally permits counsel to interpose objections. Calls for similar reform to allow witnesses the right to have counsel present during testimony have been echoed by the Cato Institute, the Capital Center for Government Law and Policy, and others

The California Association of Health Plans, the Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies, and America's Health Insurance Plans (collectively "opposition") write that drug manufacturers acknowledge their drugs are unaffordable for patients, but rather than choose to lower their prices for everyone, they point to their PAPs, which offer copay coupons. PAPs offer coupons only to a narrow set of patients, for a narrow selection of drugs, and often only for a limited time. Once the patient hits their deductible, drugmakers discontinue the patient's coupons. The opposition argues this scheme allows drugmakers to keep their underlying prices hidden from patients, while keeping their costs extremely high for employers and consumers who end up paying much more in premiums and cost-sharing. The opposition notes that the federal government considers copay coupons illegal kickbacks in federal programs like Medicare and Medicaid because these coupons induce a patient to use a specific drug. To counter the market manipulation from coupons, health plans and insurers have worked together with employers to develop programs to hold drug companies accountable, to shed light on these pricing schemes, and keep costs low for Californians. Such programs help restore the balance in the system by allowing patients to use manufacturer coupons to save money at the pharmacy counter, but does not count the amount the drug manufacturer has paid for the drug (through the coupon) towards the patient's deductible or OOP maximum. The opposition argues legislation like this bill that bans these programs by requiring health plans and insurers to count third-party payments towards an enrollee's cost sharing obligations will eliminate incentives for drug companies to lower prices. The opposition concludes that as a result, drug companies will make more money while California families and businesses continue to foot the bill through higher premiums, higher OOP expenses, and higher federal insurance subsidies

that improper governmental activity constitutes the use of the organization's official authority or influence to commit a crime, fraud, or other serious and willful violation of law, or a willful misuse of public funds, willful breach of fiduciary duty, or willful or corrupt misconduct in office. The second condition is what places the attorney in the most precarious position of weighing the duty to protect the public interest against the risk of losing his or her license to practice law due to a violation of Section 6068(e). Without the protection provided by this bill, an attorney may in fact either remain silent, or resign from his or her job. This second condition is also what the Attorney General wishes to narrow to "felony conduct." Under the third scenario, an attorney may refer the matter directly to law enforcement or an oversight official if he or she reasonably believed that the actions of urging reconsideration and referring to a higher internal authority are futile and the seriousness of the circumstances required further action in order to prevent substantial harm to the public interest or to the organization. While it may be argued that this leaves the government lawyer a lot of leeway to decide that going through the internal mechanism of rectifying a potentially harmful situation is useless (because, perhaps, an internal report may only lead to a cover-up), the lawyer would still have to make a reasonable good faith effort to assess the seriousness of the situation and to determine whether the harm to the public interest or to the organization would be substantial if he or she does nothing more. Proponents argue that without the protections provided by this bill, the attorney may remain silent, resulting perhaps in harm to the public, or resign from the job (which is the alternative currently available under Rule 3-600), resulting in harm to the lawyer personally. d. Attorney action restricted to internal report for conduct constituting willful omission to perform official duty Under this bill, where the improper governmental activity simply involves the governmental organization's agent's willful omission to perform his or her official duty, an attorney would not be protected from discipline if he or she referred the matter directly to law enforcement or other appropriate authority with oversight responsibility. This would be in keeping with the Attorney General's position that a government attorney should advise and encourage a government agency or official to take the correct course of conduct first. e. No discipline against attorney for making referral to law enforcement Under this bill, an attorney who takes the second order of action, i.e., referral to the appropriate law enforcement or government official with oversight responsibility on the matter or governmental organization or official involved, is protected from disbarment, suspension, or other discipline, provided the attorney acted reasonably and in good faith in determining the propriety of making the referral. The language of the bill states that the referral "shall not be a cause for disbarment, suspension, or other discipline." It does not provide complete immunity in that the attorney may still have to defend himself or herself in a disciplinary proceeding brought for a violation of Section 6068(e). All it means is that if the attorney proves he or she acted reasonably and in good faith in making the determination, he or she may not be subject to discipline. e. No protection for further affirmative action initiated by attorney Under , the protections provided an attorney representing a governmental organization would end with the referral to the law enforcement agency or oversight official and subsequent disclosures required by that agency or official in the execution of their oversight responsibilities. Any further action initiated by an attorney outside of those described in the bill would be subject to disciplinary proceedings and sanctions for violations of Rule 3-600 or Section 6068(e). This is appropriate, as the exception to Section 6068(e) is supposed to be very limited and designed to give the government lawyer a narrow but clear pathway to bring improper governmental activity, under appropriate conditions to the attention of appropriate officials. 3. Attorney representing government has no affirmative duty to act even with knowledge of improper government activity An attorney representing any governmental organization who learns of improper governmental activity would have no affirmative duty to take any of the actions protected from disciplinary action by the State Bar. Thus, any whistleblowing decision is left to the individual attorney on what to do or how far up the ladder of authority to go, should he or she decide to address the situation. Although much of the information provided by the author and the COPRAC analysis of the proposed amendments to Rule 3-600 refer to government lawyers or attorney-employees of governmental organizations, the language of refers to an attorney who, "in the course of representing a governmental organization?learns of improper governmental activity." This definition could cover an attorney in private practice with a contract to perform general legal services to a city on an as-needed basis, for example, as well as an attorney in private practice who is hired as outside counsel by the city council in addition to their full-time city attorney to work on a specific case, as well as the city attorney himself or herself. In a footnote, the COPRAC report clarifies that the recommended rule should apply equally to any attorney in his or her representation of governmental clients, whether the attorney is an employee of the government or is a private attorney retained by a government agency. The committee believes that significant adverse consequences would flow from a rule that distinguishes between employees and other attorneys who represent governmental clients. "Imposing a less stringent duty on in-house government attorneys than on outside attorneys retained by the government would tend to imply that employee-lawyers provide a different type of service, or fulfill a different role, than outside counsel. In addition, a rule giving less protection to the confidentiality of information held by employee-attorneys could encourage governmental agencies to use outside counsel simply because outside counsel would owe a more stringent duty of confidentiality than an in-house governmental attorney." Thus would apply to any attorney representing a governmental organization, whether in-house or not. In the case of the attorney who is hired to provide services on an as-needed basis, or the attorney whose contract is tied to a specific case, the bill does not require that the confidential information learned by the attorney be tied to the matter for which he or she was retained or hired. Thus, any "improper governmental activity" learned by the attorney, though not related to the work he or she is supposed to perform for the governmental organization, may lead the attorney to refer the matter to a law enforcement agency or higher official with oversight responsibility on the organization. The State Bar's decision in the Ossias case needs clarification Proponents contend that the case of Department of Insurance attorney Cindy Ossias demonstrated the need to clarify an attorney's right to blow the whistle, when the client is a governmental organization or official. Ms. Ossias chose to come forward and expose wrongdoing by then-Commissioner Chuck Quackenbush, at the risk of losing her license to practice law. The State Bar investigated Ms. Ossias, and ultimately exonerated her, but its decision did not clarify when disclosure by an attorney would be protected or what public policies would justify disclosure. b. Federal case law supports recognition of public agency attorney's duty to the public In re Bruce Lindsay 158 F.3d 1263 (D.C. Cir. 1998) limits the government attorney-client privilege of the President and other government officials. The court held that when government attorneys learn, through communications with their clients, of information "related to criminal misconduct," or "pertinent to possible criminal violations," the clients may not, by asserting the government attorney-client privilege, prevent such information from being disclosed to a federal grand jury. (Id at 1278.) Reasoning that the Office of the President is simply a part of the federal government like any other "consisting of government employees doing government business," the court held that there is no basis in "legal authority nor policy nor experience" to even suggest that a federal entity can maintain the "ordinary common law attorney-client privilege" to preserve the confidentiality of information relating to a federal crime. "Reason and experience, duty, and tradition dictate" that the attorney must provide the information. (Id at 1272.) c. More than half of the states allow disclosure when attorney knows of client's intent to commit a crime As originally proposed, would have mirrored Hawaii's newly-adopted rule specifically addressing issues faced by public sector attorneys. That rule, according to the Hawaii State Bar Newsletter, "recognize[s] that public agencies and public officials are drawn from the ranks of human beings who, from time to time, commit criminal or other illegal acts. Such acts are, by nature, contrary to the public good. Hawaii's version [of the model rule] makes it clear that a government lawyer's obligation of confidentiality is to be measured against the public interest, and not that of an individual or agency." A survey by the Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (PEER) shows that while most states do not distinguish between public and private attorneys when it comes to the duty of confidentiality, more than half of the states allow all attorneys to disclose a client's intent to commit a crime even if the disclosure includes revealing confidential communications. Under all of these rules (adopted by more than half the states), public sector attorneys can disclose information related to government entity wrongdoing without risking sanction by the particular state bar. In fact, California is the only state that prohibits disclosure of confidential information even when an attorney knows of the client's intent to commit a crime likely to result in death or bodily injury. Additionally, the American Bar Association has proposed amendments to Model Rule 1.6 related to confidentiality which track other states' efforts to recognize the unique duties of public agency attorneys. d. the justice courts are vestigial remains of the old justice of the peace, reformed since 1975 to assume the same jurisdiction as the municipal courts in rural areas. These historical distinctions arose primarily from practical concerns regarding access. In an era of primitive transportation, it was essential that venues for the adjudication of the daily matters of law and order be readily accessible to those traveling by foot or horseback. Consideration of serious matters entailed more time and deliberation, and the services of more sophisticated jurists whose numbers were limited: a trip to the county seat, where the higher court was located, was justified. (But even then distance was a factor in the creation of counties, with an eye to convenience: in Georgia, county lines were drawn at approximately the distance of a one day mule ride from the county seat.) With modern transportation, and with technology, the original reason for division of jurisdictions is significantly less compelling. As the demands of accessibility once drove the creation of separate types of courts, so now the demands of cost and caseload compel greater efficiencies. Separate courts naturally imply separate court administrations, leading to duplications of effort. Separate jurisdictions impose limitations on what particular judges may or may not do

There are 14 currently known "families" or classes of synthetic cannabinoids. The bill appears to include them all. The EMCDD noted that 105 individual chemicals in these classes were being monitored in Europe in 2014. This bill includes hundreds of individual chemicals in the list of prohibited synthetic cannabinoids. Many of the chemicals are identified through a letter and number combination, such as JWH-018, AM-087 and HU- 210. The letters are generally the initials of the researcher who first synthesized the chemical or the institution where the research was done. The background provided by the author and sponsor includes model statutes for prohibiting synthetic cannabinoids and synthetic stimulants. The model statute was drafted by the National Alliance for Model State Drug Laws. (http://www.namsdl.org/about.cfm.) The list of chemicals in the bill reflects the model statute. The purpose of describing synthetic cannabinoids by class or family is to include any new chemical in each class as a prohibited substance. That is, if a new drug is developed in any of the 14 classes, the chemical is prohibited, regardless of whether the individual chemical is included in the statute. It is not known whether many new synthetic cannabinoid classes can or will be developed. Synthesis of a new class or family of cannabinoids would not be included in the list of prohibited chemicals. From 2010 through 2011, reported emergency room (ER) visits linked to synthetic cannabinoids increased from 11,406 to 28,531. The vast majority of patients were young males, ages 12 through 20. (http://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/SR-1378/SR-1378.pdf) This is a relatively small number of ER visits, as total drug-related ER visits numbered 2,460,000 in 2011. Of the 2,300,000 ER visits in 2010, approximately 460,000 concerned marijuana and approximately 11,000 concerned synthetic cannabinoids. However, the reported number of synthetic cannabinoid ER visits likely understates actual visits, as testing availability is limited and some medical personnel might not be familiar with the drugs. The ER studies reported that very few patients engaged in follow-up treatment. It is not clear whether ER doctors did not make referrals for additional care, or if patients chose not to seek it. Very recently, ER visits for synthetic cannabinoids have spiked. As use of these drugs appears to be dropping, the surge in ER visits is likely the result of a dangerous change in chemical composition of the drugs. One who obtains a synthetic cannabinoid can only guess as to its composition and effects. Fundamental issues regarding ability of purchasers to seek redress Although the amendments discussed in Comments 2(b) and 3(c) arguably increase investor protection, any purchaser who loses a significant amount of his or her net worth due to an unscrupulous issuer could face difficulty in recovering the damages owed pursuant to this bill. That difficulty arises from the reality that any investor is unlikely to question a transaction as long as the business is successful (and there is a return on investment). If a business that was portrayed as promising suddenly fails (thus leaving the person with a valueless security), investors may at that point seek legal advice to examine the transaction. Thus, any investor seeking to bring an action for violation of this bill likely would be doing so against a business that is having serious financial trouble and after a potentially significant amount of time. Due to the lack of assets and potential lapsing of the applicable statute of limitations, those injured investors would appear to face significant difficulties in recovering any damages lawfully owed to them under the enforcement provisions of this bill. With respect to this issue, the Committee should consider whether the above increased investor protections sufficiently protect an investor given the potential difficulties that individuals may face when seeking to enforce those protections. Furthermore, the Committee may wish to consider whether it would be appropriate to amend the bill in order to allow a court to equitably toll the statute of limitations, and, to specifically provide that individuals directly involved in the violation are personally liable for their actions. 5. Potential preemption issues The issue has been raised that this bill may be preempted by federal law, given the passage of the Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act of 2012 (JOBS Act), and other existing provisions of federal securities laws and regulations that limit the authority of states over covered securities. The issue of federal preemption under the Supremacy Clause in the U.S. Constitution is one of both express preemption (when a federal statute explicitly confirms Congress's intention to preempt state law) and implied preemption (which can arise in two ways: where the federal law is so pervasive as to imply that Congress intended to "occupy the field" in that area of law or where there is a conflict between federal and state law). As background, the federal government has passed numerous Acts providing for federal securities laws and regulations, starting with the Securities Act of 1933 and leading up to the JOBS Act. At the same time, every state has its own securities laws, called "Blue Sky Laws," that are designed to protect investors against fraudulent sales practices and activities. While these laws can vary from state to state, most states' laws, including California's Corporate Securities Law of 1968, typically require companies making small offerings to register offerings before they can be sold in that state. Where federal law exempts registration of certain securities, Blue Sky Laws requiring registration or qualification are expressly preempted under the National Securities Market Improvement Act (NSMIA) of 1997. Thus, the issue arises as to whether the exemption created by the JOBS Act and its corresponding regulations would preempt any state laws attempting to provide for similar, but potentially conflicting, exemptions. A corporate attorney advising the author and sponsor of this bill writes that "Rule 506 of Regulation D is the only private offering exemptive rule promulgated by the SEC for which state regulation is pre-empted by Section 18. . . . is specifically authorized by federal rule 504(b)(1)(iii) which provides: '(b) Conditions to be met. (1) General conditions. To qualify for exemption under this [Section] 230.504, offers and sales must satisfy the terms and conditions of [Sections] 230.501 and 230.502 (a), (c) and (d), except that the provisions of [Section] 230.502 (c) and (d) will not apply to offers and sales of securities under this [Section] 230.504 that are made: . . .' '(iii) Exclusively according to state law exemptions from registration that permit general solicitation and general advertising so long as sales are made only to "accredited investors" as defined in [Section] 230.501(a).' Therefore, AB [2081] is not pre-empted by any law or rule . . . ." Despite this assertion, it remains unclear why Rule 506 and the impending regulations could not be construed by some to preempt this bill. To the extent that this bill is attempting to provide an alternative to the recently enacted federal law and unknown pending regulations, the determination of whether or not this bill is preempted is ultimately for the courts. 6.
